briefing.opening: Good day. We now begin the Daily Climate Briefing for November 22, 2026.

sections.title: 🔴 [COP31 Breakdown] Failure to Adopt Final Agreement for First Time in 17 Years Amid Fossil Fuel Disagreements
sections.content: The 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), held in Antalya, Türkiye, officially collapsed after negotiations dragged on two days past the scheduled closing date, failing to adopt a final agreement [35, 36, 80]. When the host nation’s final draft omitted any mention of phasing out fossil fuels—the primary driver of global warming—the EU, the UK, and other parties refused to accept it, leading to intense confrontations between 130 nations and Saudi Arabia [6, 9, 45, 56, 88]. This marks the first COP summit in 17 years to conclude without an agreement since COP15 in 2009, drawing deep disappointment and criticism from the international community, with the UN Secretary-General warning that climate science leaves no room for ambiguity [35, 48, 57].

sections.title: ⚠️ [Climate Crisis Warning] Ecosystem Degradation and the Expansion of Climate Lawsuits over the Right to Survival
sections.content: While international diplomatic negotiations face an impasse, scientific warnings continue to mount, including field observations from the Arctic and ecological transformations in Canada's boreal forests [41, 70]. The sense of crisis is also escalating among farmers on the front lines of climate change; beyond the hardships faced by farmers in Senegal, domestic farmers in South Korea have even filed climate lawsuits against corporations identified as key drivers of the crisis [8, 43]. Furthermore, as highlighted by the Turkish Hoteliers Federation, socioeconomic instability triggered by the climate crisis is intensifying daily, threatening the broader tourism sector and disrupting everyday life [44, 55].

sections.title: 🌱 [Local Carbon Neutrality] Grassroots Climate Action Led by Municipalities and Educational Institutions Bears Fruit
sections.content: Despite the gridlock in global cooperation, domestic local governments and academia continue to actively pursue field-oriented carbon neutrality initiatives [14, 22]. Voluntary efforts by local communities have yielded notable results, such as Gimhae City winning five ministerial awards and Sangju City receiving an excellence award at the 2026 Carbon Neutrality Contest [16, 21, 24]. In addition, community-based green transitions are steadily advancing, with the National Institute of Ecology completing a standard ecosystem observation network for climate response in Gotjawal, Susan-ri, Jeju, and municipalities such as Buan County and Cheonan City holding operational meetings and forums to develop tailored local models [10, 17, 20].

sections.title: 🌱 [Energy Transition] Accelerating Renewable Energy Deployment and Expanding Clean Tech Infrastructure
sections.content: The International Energy Agency (IEA) released an analysis projecting that if South Korea achieves its 100 GW renewable energy target, it could substantially reduce the nation's energy import dependence [32]. Responding to this momentum, Gwangju Metropolitan City is launching a full-scale renewable energy deployment project next year across 11,300 locations in 26 districts, and Kangwon Land has decided to expand solar power installations and introduce wind energy at its resort [31, 34]. Furthermore, supportive technologies and policies are accelerating, including trial operations of airborne wind energy systems, technical exchanges on BESS failure prevention, and the government's imminent announcement of support measures for domestic electric vehicles [30, 38, 39].

briefing.closing: Even amid the major setback of the international community's failed consensus on fossil fuels, decarbonization efforts across local communities and industrial sites continue unabated. That concludes today's climate briefing.
